fields.question: Does local TokenMinds run full production multi-context decoding?
fields.answer: No. A small GRU and SID heads preserve dual output, not Gemini scale, 15 targets, beam 40, or KV refresh serving.
fields.example: Dense and code outputs do not establish shared prefill or million-read caching.

fields.question: Why output both a dense vector and future-interest SID tokens?
fields.answer: Dense output fits existing rankers but can flatten multiple interests. Item-space SID prefixes provide several actionable clusters without prose. Future-window targets are training only.
fields.example: Represent baking and photography with separate prefixes plus a general user vector.

fields.question: Does parameter-free mixing make the whole TokenMixer-Large parameter-free?
fields.answer: No. Mix/revert are fixed rearrangements; headwise and tokenwise SwiGLU, deep residuals, and auxiliary losses still learn.
fields.example: Channel shuffling is fixed, but the FFNs processing channels train.

fields.question: What does mix–headFFN–revert add over tokenwise FFN?
fields.answer: Rearrangement exposes slices from different tokens to a nonlinear head transform, then restores layout. It is not dynamic attention, and one small gain cannot replace all attention.
fields.example: Each token can receive transformed evidence from other tokens after reverting.

fields.question: What can the local RankMixer comparison establish?
fields.answer: Match width, depth, negatives, and steps, but the result is small single-seed and lacks full attention controls. Bind FFNs to mixed positions and preserve revert order.
fields.example: The first mixed head need not be the first original feature slot.

fields.question: Why use headwise SwiGLU after mixing and tokenwise SwiGLU after revert?
fields.answer: The former learns cross-token combinations from rearranged channels; the latter refines restored per-token states. Residual intervals and intermediate supervision support depth. Rearrangement moves information but does not learn interactions.
fields.example: Mix price and preference channels, learn interactions, then restore fields for token-specific processing.

fields.question: Does tool frequency mean more calls are better?
fields.answer: No. It is a system calibration signal, not user relevance or successful-call quality. Evaluate use distribution and utility separately.
fields.example: Raising an uncommon tool's rate does not make it relevant to unrelated questions.

fields.question: How do dynamic frequency weights differ from a fixed positive/negative ratio?
fields.answer: Dynamic weights follow tool-use statistics; fixed ratios do not. Frequency is not utility, so do not trade relevance away and report only triggers.
fields.example: A low-use tool can get more opportunities only where appropriate.

fields.question: Does local ToolRec execute real tools?
fields.answer: No. MovieLens tests calibration/scoring without private sessions or tool calls. Use versioned training-window frequencies, not future test rates.
fields.example: Movie genre counts are not API cost or service load.

fields.question: Why calibrate user preference and tool frequency rather than reward triggers alone?
fields.answer: Trigger-only rewards overcall irrelevant tools; user-only optimization may ignore supply/use imbalance. Dynamic weights balance both, but frequency is governance, not quality.
fields.example: Live flight questions may need a tool, whereas definitions need not call it to boost frequency.

fields.question: Why combine lifelong and recent histories in TransAct V2?
fields.answer: Candidate retrieval finds relevant older evidence, while recent history captures immediate intent. One Transformer fuses both with candidates early.
fields.example: A current browse and a similar older interest can both support a candidate.

fields.question: How does guaranteed recent retention differ from full-history top-k?
fields.answer: It keeps fresh behavior even with low similarity, while other positions come from candidate search. Extra context costs compute; gains depend on data.
fields.example: A new interest may not rank highly under an old similarity model.

fields.question: Can Next Action Loss labels enter the current input?
fields.answer: No. Next positive behavior is supervision only; input reads the past, and negatives must be valid. Local model scope excludes production SKUT/request dedup and throughput.
fields.example: Adding the future click to history trivially leaks the auxiliary target.

fields.question: Why keep raw recent events and add Next Action Loss?
fields.answer: Candidate matching retrieves old evidence but can miss emerging intent. Keep recent events and fuse with retrieved history. NAL learns next positive action beyond CTR; missed remote events and serving performance remain separate.
fields.example: A tent candidate finds old camping while raw history shows new family-travel interest.

fields.question: Why compress source history and target tokens?
fields.answer: Source noise and many target tokens both raise cross-attention cost. Norm-aware pooling and target compression act at different ends; domain embeddings limit confusion. Compression loses detail.
fields.example: Summarize source behavior and combine target fields before interaction.

fields.question: How does norm weighting differ from averaging source tokens?
fields.answer: Larger norms get more weight, whereas mean is uniform. Norm is a proxy, not causal importance. Domain position encoding is not one shared constant.
fields.example: A high-amplitude noisy feature may receive too much influence.

fields.question: Does 85% fewer target FLOPs imply equal end-to-end latency savings?
fields.answer: No. Structural counts omit memory movement and other service stages. No original 40B interactions, large ads catalog, or ANN are reproduced.
fields.example: Preprocessing or retrieval can dominate even if attention arithmetic falls.

fields.question: Why norm-pool source history, compress target tokens, and add domain positions?
fields.answer: Norm weighting selects among noisy source events; target compression reduces cross-domain compute, while position/domain identity separates business meanings. Norm is not guaranteed relevant and compression can lose target detail.
fields.example: Mark article saves and product purchases as different while compressing both sides for ad retrieval.

fields.question: Why split behavior and request streams?
fields.answer: Cache global/local historical states asynchronously, then let short candidate requests cross-attend. Share only candidate-independent portions.
fields.example: Several candidates read one user cache but retain separate matching.

fields.question: How does shared multi-cutoff pooling compare with independent pooling?
fields.answer: Merge softmax statistics to reuse prefix work, with equivalent forward and gradients. This is compute reuse, not a changed score. Base, Retrieval, and Ranking are distinct production tests.
fields.example: Shared pooling should match independent computation on the same input.

fields.question: Why combine duplicate sparse row gradients before squaring?
fields.answer: Squaring is nonlinear: sum logical-step gradients first. Small A100 tensors verify this rule, not the 32-H200 system or an upgraded adapter grade.
fields.example: Opposite gradients should cancel before the square.

fields.question: Why cache global/local behavior and cross-attend only from the short service stream?
fields.answer: Behavior changes slower than requests, allowing historical encoding amortization. Global represents overall interests, local recent detail. Cache building/refresh still cost work, and candidate-dependent states are not public user caches.
fields.example: Reuse long history across opens and refresh local data without re-encoding years per candidate.

fields.question: Why encode business value in TSGR generation?
fields.answer: Semantic-only retrieval followed by isolated pre-ranking separates retrieval from value. Global and query-conditioned codes plus joint VRM connect generation states with fine business ranking.
fields.example: Among semantically similar items, include transaction fit for the current query.

fields.question: Why retain global and query-conditioned value codes?
fields.answer: Global summarizes broad value; conditional code expresses value for specific demand. Global can favor head items and conditional needs reliable query statistics.
fields.example: A bestseller may be worse for a specialist query than a niche product.

fields.question: What leakage must local TSGR IDs and VRM avoid?
fields.answer: Use training-period value estimates and code assignments, align query conditions with item identity, and update VRM jointly under protocol. Never encode test conversion.
fields.example: Putting a future order amount into an item code leaks the prediction target.
